lessons.title: Interest Rate Differentials and the Carry Trade

children.text: On 5 August 2024, Japan's Nikkei 225 crashed 12.4% in a single day, its worst session since 1987. The Nifty 50 fell 2.68% to 24,055.60 the same day. The trigger was not a war or a bank failure. Six days earlier, the Bank of Japan had raised its policy rate from around 0.1% to just 0.25%. A move that small shook markets from Tokyo to Dalal Street because of one of the most popular trades in global finance: borrow where money is cheap, invest where it pays more. This lesson explains how interest rate gaps pull money across borders, how the carry trade works, and why it pays slowly and loses fast.

body.text: Money flows towards higher interest rates, but only as long as the currency does not eat up the extra return. The carry trade collects the rate gap in small, steady amounts and gives it back in sudden, violent drops.

children.text: Why Interest Rate Gaps Move Currencies

markDefs.definition: The gap between interest rates in two countries, such as the RBI repo rate minus the US Fed funds rate.

children.text: Global investors constantly compare what their money earns in different countries. When Indian government bonds pay far more than US Treasuries, foreign funds have a reason to buy rupees and invest in India. That rupee demand supports the currency. When the
interest rate differential
narrows, because the US raises rates or India cuts them, some of that money leaves, and the rupee comes under pressure. Rates are not the only driver, but they are one of the most powerful.

body.title: RBI Repo Rate vs US Fed Funds Upper Bound (%)

children.text: Look at 2022. The US Fed raised rates from near zero to a 4.50% upper bound to fight inflation. RBI also hiked, from 4.00% to 6.25%, but by less. The gap between Indian and US policy rates shrank from 3.75 percentage points to 1.75. Over the same year, USD/INR rose from about 74.30 to about 82.70. Crude oil prices and the war in Ukraine played a big part too, but a shrinking rate advantage made holding rupees less rewarding just when the dollar was becoming more attractive.

body.title: The rupee in 2022
body.prompt: USD/INR moved from about 74.30 at the start of 2022 to about 82.70 at the end. By what percentage did the rupee lose value against the dollar? Enter a positive number rounded to two decimals.
body.explanation: Rupee change = 74.30 ÷ 82.70 minus 1 = 0.8984 minus 1 = minus 10.16%. Remember from Chapter 2 that the dollar's gain over the same move is bigger: 82.70 ÷ 74.30 minus 1 = 11.31%.

markDefs.definition: The interest rate minus inflation. It shows how much purchasing power an investor actually gains.

children.text: Serious investors look past the headline rate to the
real interest rate

. A 7% bond in a country with 8% inflation loses purchasing power every year, and its currency tends to weaken to reflect that. A 5% bond with 2% inflation is far more attractive in real terms. High nominal rates alone do not make a currency strong.

body.label: India's real policy rate, mid-2026 (approximate)
body.context: Repo rate of 5.25% minus RBI's FY27 CPI inflation projection of 5.0%, from the August 2026 policy. A thin real rate gives foreign investors less cushion if the rupee weakens.

children.text: The Carry Trade: Earning the Gap

markDefs.definition: The low-interest currency a carry trader borrows, such as the Japanese yen or Swiss franc.
The high-interest currency a carry trader invests in, such as the Indian rupee, Brazilian real or Mexican peso.

children.text: A carry trade has three steps. Borrow in a
funding currency
with a low interest rate. Convert the money into a
target currency

with a higher rate and invest it there. Pocket the difference, as long as the target currency does not fall by more than the gap before you convert back. Nothing about the trade is hedged. The profit depends on the exchange rate behaving.

body.latex: \text{Carry return} \approx (r_{\text{target}} - r_{\text{funding}}) - \text{Fall in the target currency}
body.caption: The rate gap is what you earn. Currency depreciation is what can take it away.

children.text: Worked example with illustrative one-year rates: a global fund borrows $10 million at 3.75%, converts it at USD/INR 95.50 into ₹95.50 crore, and invests in Indian government securities yielding 6.00%. After one year it has ₹101.23 crore and owes $10.375 million. Whether it made money depends entirely on where USD/INR is when it converts back.

body.caption: Outcome of the $10 million rupee carry trade after one year

body.title: When the rupee slides
body.prompt: Using the same trade, ₹101.23 crore to convert back and $10,375,000 owed, suppose USD/INR is 99.00 after one year. How many dollars does the fund lose? Enter a positive number rounded to the nearest dollar.
body.explanation: ₹1,01,23,00,000 ÷ 99.00 = $10,225,253. The fund owes $10,375,000, so it loses $149,747. A fall of about 3.5% in the rupee (95.50 to 99.00) wiped out the 2.25 percentage point rate gap and then some.

body.title: Why the break-even rate equals the forward rate

children.text: The break-even of 97.57 is not a coincidence. In the previous lesson you priced the one-year forward with the same rates, 6.00% and 3.75%, and got exactly 97.57. That means if the fund had hedged by selling rupees one year forward, it would have locked in precisely break-even, earning nothing extra over the US rate.

This is the key insight: a fully hedged carry trade earns nothing, because the forward premium eats the rate gap. The carry trade only makes money if the rupee falls by less than the forward premium implies. A carry trader is really betting that the future spot rate will beat the forward rate.

body.text: Textbook theory, called uncovered interest parity, says high-interest currencies should weaken by roughly the rate gap over time, leaving no free profit. In the real world, over months and even years, they often weaken by less or not at all. That is why carry trades are popular. But when fear hits, high-yield currencies can fall several percent in days as everyone exits at once. Traders describe carry as picking up coins in front of a steamroller.

children.text: Case Study: The Yen Carry Trade Unwind of August 2024

For years, Japan kept interest rates at or below zero. Funds borrowed yen almost free, sold it for dollars, Mexican pesos and other higher-yielding assets, and even bought technology stocks. All that yen selling weakened the yen, which made the trade look even better. By early July 2024, one dollar bought about 161.6 yen, the weakest the yen had been in 38 years. Then the funding currency started to rise, and the trade reversed all at once.

body.title: How the Yen Carry Trade Unravelled

events.title: Yen at a 38-year low
events.description: USD/JPY reaches about 161.6. Borrowing in yen and investing elsewhere looks like easy money.

events.title: Bank of Japan hikes
events.description: The policy rate rises from around 0.1% to 0.25%, and the central bank signals more tightening. Borrowing yen suddenly looks riskier.

events.title: Weak US jobs data
events.description: The US adds only 114,000 jobs against expectations of about 175,000, raising bets on Fed rate cuts. The US-Japan rate gap looks set to shrink from both sides.

events.title: The unwind
events.description: Funds rush to buy back yen to repay loans. USD/JPY falls to about 142, the Nikkei crashes 12.4%, the S&P 500 drops about 3%, and the Nifty 50 falls 2.68%.

children.text: Why did a tiny rate change cause a crash? Leverage and crowding. When the yen rose, every carry trader's debt got bigger in dollar terms at the same time. Many had to sell whatever they owned, including shares, to buy yen and repay. That forced selling pushed the yen higher still, triggering more selling. The Nifty fell not because anything changed in India, but because global funds were raising cash everywhere.

body.title: Danger for a yen carry trader
body.question: A fund has borrowed yen at a very low rate to invest in higher-yielding US assets. Which event is most dangerous for this position?
options: The US Fed raises interest rates
The Bank of Japan raises interest rates and the yen strengthens sharply
The Japanese yen weakens further against the dollar
US bond yields rise while Japanese rates stay at zero
body.explanation: A yen carry trader owes yen. If Japanese rates rise and the yen strengthens, the loan costs more and is worth more in dollars at the same time. The other three events widen the rate gap or weaken the yen, which help the trade.

children.text: India as a Carry Destination

The rupee is a classic target currency: higher interest rates than developed markets, a large bond market, and an RBI that damps volatility. The inclusion of Indian government bonds in JP Morgan's emerging-market bond index from June 2024 brought more foreign money into rupee debt. But that same money is quick to leave when the rate gap narrows or the rupee starts falling fast, which is exactly when RBI has to spend reserves to steady things.

body.title: What draws carry money into the rupee vs what pushes it out

columns.label: Pulls money in
points: A wide gap between Indian and US yields
Low and falling Indian inflation, which lifts real rates
A stable rupee backed by large RBI reserves
Global index inclusion and calm risk sentiment

columns.label: Pushes money out
points: US rate hikes or RBI rate cuts that shrink the gap
Rising Indian inflation that erodes real returns
A sharp rupee fall, often triggered by crude oil spikes
Global panic, when funds sell risky assets everywhere

body.text: Carry trades by funds are leveraged and professionally risk-managed, and they still blow up. Do not try to copy them through offshore forex apps, which are not a legal route for Indian residents. And be wary of any pitch offering a high "guaranteed" return in a foreign currency or crypto token. If the return is high, the currency or credit risk behind it is high too.

body.title: The NRI deposit decision
body.scenario: Farhan, an engineer in Dubai, has $50,000 to park for one year in India. His bank offers an NRE rupee fixed deposit at 6.75% or an FCNR(B) US dollar deposit at 4.50% (illustrative rates). USD/INR is 95.50 today. Assume interest on both is tax-free for him and there are no conversion costs.
body.prompt: Which option is effectively a carry trade? Work out the USD/INR level after one year at which both options give him the same result, and explain how he should think about the choice.
body.modelAnswer:
1. The NRE deposit is the carry trade: he converts dollars into rupees to earn the higher rupee rate and takes the risk that the rupee falls.
2. NRE: $50,000 × 95.50 = ₹47,75,000, growing at 6.75% to ₹50,97,312.50 after a year.
3. FCNR(B): $50,000 grows at 4.50% to $52,250, with no currency risk in dollar terms.
4. Break-even: ₹50,97,312.50 ÷ $52,250 = USD/INR of about 97.56. If the rupee is stronger than 97.56 in a year, the NRE deposit wins. If USD/INR is above 97.56, the FCNR(B) deposit wins.
5. That break-even is a rise of about 2.15% in USD/INR, close to the 2.25 percentage point rate gap. The rupee fell by more than that in some years, such as 2022, and by less in others. If Farhan will eventually spend the money in India, the NRE deposit matches his needs. If he may need dollars back, the FCNR(B) deposit avoids a currency bet.

body.title: Name the borrowed currency
body.textWithBlank: In a carry trade, the low-interest currency that is borrowed is called the ___ currency.
body.explanation: The funding currency is borrowed cheaply, historically the yen or Swiss franc. The target currency is the higher-yielding one the money is invested in.

cards.definition: The gap between two countries' interest rates. A wider gap in India's favour tends to attract foreign capital to the rupee.
Nominal interest rate minus inflation. What investors actually gain in purchasing power.
Borrowing a low-interest currency to invest in a high-interest one, unhedged, to earn the rate gap.
The cheap currency borrowed in a carry trade, such as the yen.
The theory that high-interest currencies should weaken by the rate gap over time. It often fails in the short run.
A rush to close carry trades, which strengthens funding currencies and hits risky assets, as in August 2024.

points: Higher interest rates attract foreign capital and support a currency. A narrowing rate gap tends to push money out.
In 2022, the gap between the RBI repo rate and the US Fed rate shrank from 3.75 to 1.75 percentage points, and the rupee lost about 10% against the dollar.
Investors care about real rates, interest minus inflation, not just headline rates.
A carry trade borrows a low-rate currency, invests in a high-rate one, and earns the gap only if the target currency does not fall too much.
The break-even rate of an unhedged carry trade equals the forward rate. Hedging removes both the risk and the extra return.
Carry pays small, steady returns and loses big when fear strikes, as the August 2024 yen unwind showed.
The rupee is a popular carry destination, which means foreign bond money can leave quickly when conditions change.

Policy rates and market levels are approximate and as of the dates stated. NRIs should check current deposit rates and tax treatment with their bank and a tax adviser.
